extracted.intended_audience: research authors using Review Commons / preparing refereed preprints for journal submission (and journal editors who will assess them)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors preparing a Revision Plan (or Full Revision) to accompany a Review Commons refereed preprint so journal editors can judge what additional work will be done, what has already been done, and what authors will not do. Focuses on communicating planned experiments/analyses, completed changes, and justifications for declines.

rubrics_metrics.name: General statement / abbreviated post-review cover letter
rubrics_metrics.description: A revision plan begins with a general statement – authors may, for example, write about the study’s goal, and its main conclusions, or highlight aspects of the reviewers’ comments. It could be considered an abbreviated, post-review cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this opening to orient the editor to the paper’s aims and main takeaways and to flag major reviewer concerns. Be concise but informative; treat it as a high-level summary that frames the detailed plan that follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed point-by-point plan of additional experiments and analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors then present to editors a detailed point-by-point plan of the additional experiments and analyses they will perform to respond to reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe concrete actions (which experiments/analyses, timelines, expected outcomes) that will be done before engaging in new experimentations and analyses. The purpose is to allow editors to make informed decisions about how suitable the revised version is likely to be for their journal, saving time for both authors and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of revisions already completed
rubrics_metrics.description: In the third section, the authors point out which revisions have already been done in response to reviewer comments – these are often minor text edits, alternate analysis of pre-existing data, or data not included in the first draft, but which already existed. These changes have been incorporated into the revised manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify which reviewer requests were addressed without new data collection, indicate exactly where changes appear in the revised manuscript, and note whether changes involve reanalysis of existing data, text edits, or newly included (but previously available) data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of which reviewer-requested changes will not be performed and why
rubrics_metrics.description: The final section is where authors can state clearly, in detail, which additional experiments, analyses, or changes to the manuscript requested by reviewers they do not wish to perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete reasons (technical limitations such as unavailable materials; excessive cost or time; need for new collaborations; or principled disagreement with the necessity/logic of the request). Being explicit lets editors judge whether omitted work is essential for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give editors information to judge fit to journal scope and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The revision plan highlights the elements of refereed preprint that are crucial for a journal editor – they now need to fit the refereed preprint to the scientific scope and quality bar of their journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the plan on the issues most relevant to editorial decisions about scope and rigor. Emphasize how proposed revisions will raise the manuscript to the journal’s expected standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Full Revision template for traditional point-by-point responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Full Revision template is essentially equivalent to the traditional point-by-point response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors already have a final, fully revised manuscript, use this simpler template to map reviewer comments to specific changes made in the revision (classic response format).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses should be detailed, explanatory, and respectful
rubrics_metrics.description: A productive peer review process requires not only high-quality (and respectful) reviewer comments but also a detailed response from the authors to explain how issues can be resolved, dissipate potential misunderstandings, and provide arguments when opinions diverge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address each substantive comment clearly: explain how you will resolve the issue or why you disagree, provide evidence or rationale for disagreements, and keep tone professional and constructive to facilitate scientific debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about technical or practical limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can say they do not wish to perform certain requests due to technical limitations – for example when materials are unavailable when the experiments are considered too costly or time-consuming, require the establishment of new collaborations, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When declining requests, give specific, factual constraints (e.g., unobtainable reagents, prohibitive cost, time constraints, collaborator dependency) so editors can weigh the necessity of the omitted work rather than speculate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use templates across journals to save time (reusability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like all elements of the refereed preprint package, these templates can be used at different journals, saving time in the resubmission process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the revision plan so it is modular and portable across journals (clear sections: summary, planned work, completed changes, declined items) to streamline multiple submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make refereed preprint package transparent (expose reviews and replies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The refereed preprint accelerates the public dissemination of peer-reviewed research. Review Commons exposes reviews and authors’ replies to provide transparent access to the full extent of the scientific discourse, with its complexities and subtleties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that reviews and responses will be public: craft replies that are informative for the broader community and demonstrate that reviewer concerns have been considered; journals will still perform final quality assurance on adequacy of responses.
